source: Superforecasting reality check: Evidence from a small pool of experts and expedited identification (2020)
finding: A small GJP-style tournament (9 months, 14 questions) found a few forecasters who stayed on top from an identification phase to a confirmation phase. Weak, partial replication of persistence.
numbers: 314 registered, 195 fully engaged (64%). 6 identification questions, 8 confirmation questions. Confirmed at top 2%: 2 people (1 per training group). Confirmed at 5%/10%/25%: 8/16/38. Rule: top bin on at least 5 of 6 questions, then at least 6 of 8.
limits: Own stricter per-question rank rule, not the GJP rule. No luck null (permutation) test is reported, so 2 confirmed people at top 2% of 195 is not shown to beat chance. One EU country, 67.7% academics, incentive was a free 650 EUR course. Questions written by the authors. Authors call it supportive.
agent_relevance: Persistence of a top quarter is easy to find; persistence of a top 2% is thin at small N. If we pick a best scaffold on a few questions, expect much of the lead to be luck.

source: Superforecasting reality check (2020): extra training arm
finding: Group B got 20 extra minutes (forecast decomposition and structured analogies) on top of the 40-minute GJP training. It did not produce significantly more top forecasters.
numbers: Group A n=86 (standard 40 min), Group B n=109 (60 min). Top 2%: 1 vs 1. Top 10%: 7 vs 9. Top 25%: 14 vs 24, not significant. Median standardized Brier -0.252 (A) vs -0.437 (B). Bootstrap stochastic dominance favoured B on all four metrics.
limits: Unequal group sizes after drop-out (64% retention). The 100 x 20 bootstrap is not a standard test. Not randomised after drop-out. No effect on the headline count.
agent_relevance: Adding training-style content gives at most a small shift of the whole distribution, not a new class of top performers. Matches the shrinking Chang 2016 effect (K06).

source: Superforecasting reality check (2020): who ended up in the top quartile
finding: In the top 25% (n=38), chi-square tests linked membership to being male, 16-20 years of experience, advanced English, daily news reading, and English-language internet sources.
numbers: Male 24.2% in top bin vs female 11.3% (chi2(1)=4.81, p<.05). Daily information gathering 31.8%, weekly 20.9%, monthly 14.3%, rarer 3.6%, never 0%. English sources 24.4% vs 8.3% without (chi2(1)=6.87).
limits: Many uncorrected chi-square tests on n=38 of 195 people; not preregistered. The gender result is not a GJP finding and is likely sample-specific.
agent_relevance: Frequency of information intake points the same way as GJP's activity finding. For an LLM, retrieval breadth and refresh rate are the analogue; demographic traits are not.

source: Hauenstein, Thomas, Illingworth and Dougherty (2024/2025) Rethinking the Role of Teams and Training in Geopolitical Forecasting: The Effect of Uncontrolled Method Variance on Statistical Conclusions. Psychological Science
finding: An independent re-analysis of the first two GJP years with item response theory says the Mellers 2014 teaming and training effects depend on uncontrolled method variables. Best-fit models include extraneous variables that cut or reverse the effects. A strategic-responding trait also separates superforecasters from others.
numbers: Seven IRT models compared over the first 2 years, three ways of conditioning the data. In all cases the best model included one or more extraneous variables that substantially eliminated, reduced, and in some cases even reversed the teaming and training effects. Effect sizes are in the full text, which I could not open.
limits: I read the Europe PMC and OSF abstracts only; the full text (Sage returned 403, OSF page empty) was not available. Names of the extraneous variables not confirmed. Authors are not the GJP group (author names from Crossref). A challenge to the causal reading, not a new tournament.
agent_relevance: Weakens K06 and K08: training and teaming gains may partly reflect which questions people chose and how they answered. Do not build the schema on training works because it is training.

source: Mellers, Baker, Chen, Mandel and Tetlock (2017) How generalizable is good judgment? A multi-task, multi-benchmark study. Judgment and Decision Making 12(4)
finding: Superforecasters tied or beat regular forecasters and undergraduates on consistency, discrimination and coherence lab tasks, so good judgment seems moderately unified. This is the main outside-the-tournament check on whether forecasting skill is a stable trait.
numbers: Survey 1: 173 superforecasters (69% response), 75 regular forecasters (48%), 92 undergraduates. Survey 2: 67 supers (52%), 90 regulars (47%), 186 undergraduates. Cross-measure correlations .08 to .39, mean .20. Composite vs superforecaster status: biserial .46 (S1) and .60 (S2); .73 and .82 after correction for unreliability.
limits: Cross-sectional. Supers were selected on the same Brier criterion; no later-year follow-up. Response rates under 70%. The extracted text has no year-to-year .65 and no 70% retention figure (searched persist, retain, year-to-year, .65).
agent_relevance: Silver standards (consistency under rewording, discrimination, coherence) are cheap to test in an LLM and K21 already links consistency to Brier; this paper gives the human prior of r about .2 between such measures.

source: Mellers et al. (2017) introduction: what earlier GJP papers said about persistence
finding: The authors summarise the persistence result in words, not numbers: the top 2% each year were named superforecasters and worked in elite teams, became more accurate and resisted regression to the mean (citing Mellers 2015b). They also cite Goldstein et al. (2016): supers beat US intelligence analysts by roughly 30% on Brier.
numbers: No year-to-year correlation or retention percentage in this paper. All supers had at least a college degree, about two thirds post-graduate. Superforecasters always worked in teams.
limits: Secondary summary by the same research group. The .65 and 70% figures remain only in the 2015 book (critique gap 4).
agent_relevance: Gap 4 stays open for a primary table: no GJP-family paper I could open gives .65 or 70%.

source: Tetlock (2005) Expert Political Judgment, via the Wikipedia profile of the author
finding: Pre-GJP baseline: 284 experts, forecasts 1984-2003, about 28,000 predictions. Experts were only slightly better than chance and usually worse than simple extrapolation, especially 3-5 years out. Hedgehogs did worse than foxes, and media-famous experts were among the least accurate.
numbers: 284 experts; about 28,000 forecasts; 1984 to 2003.
limits: SECOND-HAND: Wikipedia, not the book. Calibration and discrimination indices and dilettante-vs-algorithm comparisons are not given and I did not invent them. The book was not opened.
agent_relevance: Pre-GJP baseline: selection, aggregation and feedback, not expertise, raised accuracy. Gap 9 only partly closed.

source: Schoenegger, Jones, Tetlock and Mellers (2025) Prompt Engineering Large Language Models' Forecasting Capabilities. arXiv 2506.01578
finding: 38 prompts on four LLMs (Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Claude 3.5 Haiku, GPT-4o, Llama 3.1 405B) on ForecastBench questions. In the preregistered mixed model only two prompts differ from control, both worse. In simpler paired t-tests three base-rate-type prompts help a little.
numbers: About 3,636-3,771 usable forecasts per model. Mixed model: Bayesian Reasoning +0.030 Brier (p<.001), Propose-Evaluate-Select +0.033 (p<.001); other prompts within about +/-0.011, adjusted p about .77-.80. Paired t-tests after Benjamini-Hochberg: Frequency-Based Reasoning, Base Rate First (-0.016, SD 0.106, n=390), Step-Back better; 8 prompts better before correction. Study 2 (compound prompts, o1, o1-mini): Brier 0.217 and 0.216, no compound prompt clearly better.
limits: Single-paragraph prompts only. The claim none beat noise (K16) holds for the preregistered mixed model but is too strong for the t-test analysis, where three base-rate-style prompts survive correction with small effects (about 1 to 1.6 Brier points on the 0-1 scale).
agent_relevance: Reference-class prompts are the only CHAMPS KNOW element with any LLM support; explicit Bayes instructions hurt. Update K16 to say so.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2025) prompt paper: forecast decisiveness (gap 7)
finding: Harmful prompts pushed forecasts away from 0.5 more, but so did Chain of Thought, which was not significantly harmful. So distance from 0.5 alone does not explain the harm.
numbers: Mean distance from 0.5: Bayesian Reasoning, Propose-Evaluate-Select, Chain of Thought 17.2 to 19.9 percentage points; Control, Re-Reading, Anti-Biasing 11.9 to 13.4 points. Mean forecast Bayesian Reasoning 0.476 (SD 0.250), Base Rate First 0.428 (SD 0.207). Authors suggest superficial mimicry of Bayesian updating.
limits: Correlational across prompts; the mechanism is the authors' guess. Distance from 0.5 was not manipulated directly.
agent_relevance: Test: leave the update step free-form, then apply an external recalibration (d13) rather than asking the model to do Bayes in the prompt.

source: Lu (2025) Evaluating LLMs on Real-World Forecasting Against Expert Forecasters. arXiv 2507.04562 v3
finding: Re-read for gaps 1 and 6. Each model score uses 5 separate API calls averaged. Experts were relabelled expert forecasters because Superforecaster is a registered trademark. No later version redoes the expert comparison with mean Brier on identical questions.
numbers: 464 Metaculus questions, Jul-Dec 2024. Experts answered 157 questions (47%) and 41 of the held-out set (31%). o3 .1352 main set; o3-pro .1307 on the 41-question hold-out (checked in text). Paper cites a 50 percent noise level, 50 questions, noisy forecaster wins 24% of the time result from a secondary source (Nikos 2023) that I could not trace.
limits: arXiv lists v1 6 Jul, v2 1 Aug, v3 4 Aug 2025; the abstract page does not say what changed. No FRI or Metaculus follow-up found (WebSearch budget was exhausted). The 24% figure is second-hand.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 stays open. Keep K20 contested. Do not use the experts-far-ahead headline.

source: Alur et al. (2025) AIA Forecaster: Technical Report (Bridgewater AIA Labs). arXiv 2511.07678: ensembling
finding: Averaging independent forecasts of the same system beats a single sample, with diminishing returns after a handful. A single sample stays variable even over 1,610 questions.
numbers: FB-7-21 Brier: single random forecast .1182; simple mean of 10 .1140; trimmed mean .1142; median .1138. On MarketLiquid (1,610 questions) Brier falls sharply from 1 to 5 forecasts and modestly to 15 (bootstrap from 50 forecasts per question). Authors adopt 10.
limits: Compares 1 vs 10 samples, so cost is 10x: NOT an equal-token test against one long chain. No length-matched single-chain arm. Industry report, not peer reviewed.
agent_relevance: Supports sampling-and-averaging as the cheap robust step (mechanism behind K13). Gap 2 stays open: no equal-token comparison against a long chain.

source: AIA Forecaster report: supervisor agent versus plain mean
finding: A supervisor that finds disagreements among 10 forecasts, searches to resolve them, and replaces the mean only when highly confident, beat the other synthesis methods. Letting an LLM simply pick the best forecast did worst.
numbers: FB-7-21 Brier (Table 10): agentic supervisor .1125; non-agentic (Halawi-style) .1168; best-of-k .1191; none .1199. Best-of-k picked among the 3 worst candidates 7.2% of the time. Agentic supervisor at least as good as the top 3 individual forecasts in 33.9% of cases.
limits: The no-aggregation mean differs between Table 9 (.1140) and Table 10 (.1199), so gaps across tables are unreliable. Supervisor adds search calls, so cost is not equal. Single benchmark. Murphy 2026 found LLM-judge aggregation worse than the mean (d17).
agent_relevance: Reconciling disagreement with new evidence beats picking a winner; but results conflict across benchmarks, so keep plain mean as default.

source: AIA Forecaster report: Platt scaling and log-odds extremizing (gap 8)
finding: Extremizing is a form of Platt scaling (log odds times a constant). On FB-7-21 a fixed coefficient of sqrt(3), about 1.73, gave nearly all the gain with no fitting. Fitting on another benchmark helped less than the fixed value.
numbers: FB-7-21 Brier: no correction .1119 (in-distribution column); Platt fixed .1076; Platt fitted leave-one-out .1071; fitted on the Halawi data (out of distribution) .1104; OLS .1097 ID, .1134 OOD; log-odds extremizing fixed .1085. Same Platt coefficient applied to superforecasters is best at 1.72; for AIA best at 2.27 (not used). Biggest gains in the 0.2-0.4 and 0.6-0.8 forecast bins. Text says isotonic regression and OLS are less competitive.
limits: Gain assumes forecasts are already on the right side of 0.5. One benchmark; the out-of-distribution fit gains only about .0015 over no correction. The fixed value comes from a theory paper (Neyman and Roughgarden 2022) that I did not open. Table layout scrambled in extraction.
agent_relevance: Optimum factor was not stable (1.72 for supers, 2.27 for AIA, weak when fitted elsewhere). Use a mild fixed factor and check on held-out questions; do not trust a factor fitted on few questions.

source: AIA Forecaster report: comparison with superforecasters on matching questions
finding: On ForecastBench variants the AIA system matched the superforecaster median on the same questions, but did not beat market prices on harder liquid-market questions.
numbers: Brier FB-7-21: AIA .1076, supers median .1110, supers mean .1123, public median .1451, o3 .133. FB-8-14: AIA .1099 vs supers .1152, public .1510. FB-Market: AIA .0753 vs supers .0740 vs market .0965. MarketLiquid (1,610 q): AIA .1258 vs market .1106. Supers answered a median of 8 per question (minimum 3).
limits: Authors built the system. Super baseline is 3 to 8 people per question. ForecastBench questions are easier than liquid markets. Authors say AIA is statistically indistinguishable from supers, not better.
agent_relevance: Scaffolded LLM about equal to supers on same-question mean Brier (ForecastBench), versus the older gap of .026 (K14). The difference is search, ensembling and calibration. Use as target level.

source: Aitchison, Jeen, Shevlane and Day (2026) Diversity is the Strength of the AI Crowd. arXiv 2606.29661 (ICML 2026 workshop)
finding: At a fixed sample count, forecasts from different models beat repeated samples from the best model, because frontier LLM probabilities are highly correlated. Relevant to gap 2: same-model samples add little.
numbers: 113 binary Metaculus AI Benchmark Q2 2025 questions. Budget B=5, 101 valid allocations enumerated. Optimal: fine-tuned gpt-oss-120b x2, Gemini 3 Pro x1, GPT-5 x1, Grok 4 x1. Removing Grok 4 costs about 1.7 baseline points, the fine-tuned model about 0.6, GPT-5 or Gemini under 0.1 each. Grok 4 was third in solo score.
limits: One tournament, N=113, at most 3 runs per model, no bootstrap confidence intervals (authors call the ranking robust, magnitudes indicative). Authors from Mantic. Equal samples, not equal tokens; across-model diversity, not across-prompt.
agent_relevance: Diversity beats depth. For a single agent the nearest analogue is prompt, role and retrieval-path diversity, but only model diversity was tested.

source: Murphy (2026) Agentic forecasting with structured linguistic beliefs (Bayesian Linguistic Forecaster). arXiv 2604.18576 v5: variance and paired design (gap 1)
finding: Question difficulty explains most of the score variance; method choice explains little. So scaffolds must be compared on the same questions with a paired design.
numbers: Two-way ANOVA, 12 methods x 400 questions x 5 trials (23,853 trials): question 62.2% of variance, method 2.7%, residual 35.1% (method F=164.5). 400 ForecastBench question-date instances (355 distinct questions, 791 resolved events). Residual leakage about 1.5% of retained search results.
limits: Descriptive ANOVA on pooled configurations, not a test of one pair. No test-retest across disjoint question sets reported.
agent_relevance: With method share of variance about 3%, small scaffold differences need paired tests and many questions. See d19.

source: Murphy (2026) BLF: trial averaging, shrinkage, Platt (gaps 2 and 8)
finding: Averaging K=5 trials improves Brier Index with more K; logit averaging gives a small extra gain. Cross-validated shrinkage chose no shrinkage. Platt scaling and hierarchical calibration gave no statistically resolved gain for the main backbone.
numbers: Platt gave +0.72 / +1.48 Brier Index with / without the crowd anchor on a preliminary model; hierarchical +0.98 / +1.80. Main backbone: no statistically resolved overall BI gain. BLF beat the crowd+empirical-prior baseline by +3.4 overall BI, significant in one tranche only. LLM-judge aggregation of reasoning traces (the AIA supervisor design) worked worse than simple mean on this benchmark.
limits: Preliminary results not shown. Market questions include crowd-price anchors that already calibrate. Conflicts with the AIA supervisor gain, so aggregation effects are benchmark-dependent.
agent_relevance: Extremizing helps when no strong external anchor exists; with a market price in context little is left to fix. Match the recalibration step to whether the agent sees a crowd number.

source: Murphy (2026) BLF: memory ablation (gap 3, partial)
finding: Carrying the full history of prior reasoning steps did not beat a compact Markov belief state (probability plus evidence summary) within a question. This is not a cross-question track record test.
numbers: 100 fresh questions (50 market, 50 dataset), K=2. Brier Index: full history 72.72, Markov 75.12, difference +2.40, 95% CI [-0.17, 4.36]; every interval includes zero.
limits: Within-question memory only. No experiment gives the agent its own per-domain Brier history. Small N.
agent_relevance: A compact summarised state is not worse than the full transcript. Gap 3 (running per-domain track record) remains untested for LLMs.

source: Derived calculation (this run): questions needed to tell two scaffolds apart (gap 1)
finding: Using paired-difference standard deviations seen in d08 (about 0.10 to 0.17 per question), a two-sided 5% test with 80% power needs hundreds to over a thousand questions for a Brier gap of about 0.01.
limits: My own calculation; independent questions assumed. SDs come from single-sample prompt contrasts; averaging 5-10 samples per question lowers SD, so N falls. No published scaffold-vs-scaffold test-retest on disjoint sets found.
agent_relevance: Plan: at least 5 samples per question, paired design on identical questions, about 300 questions before claiming a 0.02 gain; a 0.01 gain is not detectable with a few hundred.

source: EvoForesight (2026) Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting. arXiv 2610.29784
finding: An agent that turns its own resolved-prediction trajectories into reusable skills climbs the live FutureX leaderboard. Nearest published test of learning from a running record; only the abstract was read.
numbers: Up to 195% rating improvement on FutureX; first among all systems three weeks in a row; top three across four base LLMs; up to 10.7 Bradley-Terry points over the strongest baseline. No Brier or question counts on the abstract page.
limits: Abstract only. Leaderboard rating, not Brier. Not a clean track-record ablation.
agent_relevance: Outcome feedback can be distilled into skills, not just kept as raw history. Gap 3 stays open until a Brier ablation is read.
